Chapter 7: The Anatomy of Collusion—How Mutual Blame Keeps Us Stuck.
Sometimes, it’s not just one person feeling trapped—it’s the whole relationship. When two people are both stuck in their own boxes, their stories about each other start feeding off one another. That’s how a cycle forms, and breaking out of it can feel impossible.
So, what exactly is this cycle? It’s called collusion. Each person’s need to justify themselves just makes the other double down even harder. Before you know it, both are locked in, and nobody’s budging.
Think about two colleagues. Each one is sure the other is impossible to work with. One believes, “She never listens to me.” The other feels, “He’s always criticizing everything I do.” Every meeting becomes a minefield, and each is waiting for the other to mess up. Even a tiny misunderstanding turns into proof that the other really is the problem. The more each one tries to defend themselves, the more the other feels attacked. And round and round it goes.
But it doesn’t stop at work. You’ll see this pattern show up in marriages, friendships, even between parents and kids. Everyone feels completely justified. It’s so easy to think, “If only they would change, everything would be better.” But here’s the twist—the more you push, the more pushback you get.
What we usually miss is how our own actions invite the response we’re afraid of. The colleague who feels unheard? They stop listening, too. The partner who feels unappreciated? They stop showing appreciation. The parent who feels disrespected? They get more controlling. Every move we make just convinces the other person that their story is right.
So, how do you break out of this loop? It takes more than just wanting things to be better. Someone has to make the first move—to step out of their box, see the other person as a real human being, and let go of the blame. It’s not about pretending the problems aren’t there. It’s about breaking the pattern and making room for something different.
Let me share an example. There was this manager, totally stuck in a long-running conflict with a direct report. Instead of sticking to their usual defenses, the manager tried something new. They asked, “What’s it like for you, working with me?” At first, it was awkward. But slowly, the tension started to melt. Both realized they’d been caught in a loop of blaming each other. With that awareness, they began to rebuild trust, one conversation at a time.
Here’s the thing—most of us wait for the other person to change first. But nothing shifts until someone is willing to go first. That means risking a little vulnerability, really listening, and seeing the other’s humanity. It’s not easy, and it might not change things overnight. But with time, these small, brave steps can transform even the toughest relationships.
